items.author: Paul Farrelly

items.text:
Published Sep 23, 2026, 6:21 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

Gamers are no strangers to delays. In fact, if you want to call yourself a true gamer, you need a hardened heart when it comes to release windows. We've seen Grand Theft Auto VI delayed twice, with the original release date being nearly a year ago. And many Duke Nukem fans (all twelve of them) were left waiting longer than it takes to complete a masters in rocket science. Both of those sets of fans, though, have it way better than those waiting for a Half-Life 2 sequel! Delays seem inevitable and, unfortunately, The Legend of Zelda has just been hit with one.

Fear not, though The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time fans, this latest delay has nothing to do with the upcoming remake. This applies more to literary fans of our Hyrule hero. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Secrets of the Zonai is a collector's book filled with behind the scenes sketches, artwork and glorious illustrations that cover lore and history lifted straight from Hyrule. The fictional history book is an amazing companion piece for any The Legend of Zelda fan and, unfortunately, fans outside of Japan will have to wait a lot longer than first expected.

Dark Horse Direct

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Secrets of the Zonai was initially due to release in October 2026 but has now been pushed six months to April 2027. As the book is based on the existing Japanese book, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom Master Works, published by Tokuma Shoten it seems a little unfair that fans outside of Japan have been kept waiting so long. It would seem that getting localization spot on and avoiding lore getting lost in translation takes a long time to perfect.

Fans of The Legend of Zelda franchise are a bit upset learning about the latest delay. The gorgeous artwork from The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, backed up with lore from the series, sounds like the perfect Christmas gift for any budding Nintendo fan, and it would have made sense to launch it this year to tie in with the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda franchise, but alas, it's not to be. Fans are voicing their frustrations over on Reddit.

One said the following about the delay:

What is happening to this book!? It came out in Japan August 2024, what is in this book that takes 3 years to localize?

While another was happy to have a little bit more time to save up, saying the following:

I know it’s upsetting to a lot of people, but it’s a relief to me. My poor wallet is spending so much on Zelda soon that it can afford to wait a little while before this releases!

Dark Horse Direct

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake still to come in 2026, perhaps a delay will give fans more time to smash a few pots and find more rupees to purchase The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Secrets of the Zonai next April. With Grand Theft Auto VI, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of TIme remake and Gears of War: E-Day still to come in 2026, no matter what console you own, you'll be handing over your hard-earned cash before the holiday season is out.

The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Secrets of the Zonai is available to pre-order today over at Dark Horse Direct. Yes, the delay may suck for hardcore fans of The Legend of Zelda franchise, but all good things come to those who wait. This collector's item looks like the perfect coffee table conversation starter and might be the perfect companion piece to the upcoming The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of TIme remake. At the very least, it'll look good sitting next to that giant replica Master Sword you know you shouldn't have bought!

items.title: Diablo 5 will 'take a somewhat different approach' to Diablo 4's monster level scaling so your character feels noticeably stronger as you progress
items.author: Tyler Colp
items.summary: Despite its surprise announcement at BlizzCon earlier this month, Diablo 5 is a whole three years away. Blizzard's brief teaser trailer had zero gameplay in
items.text:
Despite its surprise announcement at BlizzCon earlier this month, Diablo 5 is a whole three years away. Blizzard's brief teaser trailer had zero gameplay in it, which means the action RPG sequel is still mostly a mystery.

But director Joe Shely helped paint a picture of what the real thing might look like during a recent group interview with PC Gamer.

One of the somewhat controversial aspects of the last couple Diablo games is how they handle monster difficulty. In Diablo 2, each area has a level range that determines how tough enemies will be compared to your character. Diablo 3 and Diablo 4 ditched this approach for a system that has monsters scale in difficulty as your character levels up.

In a genre all about the power fantasy of slowly becoming a demon-slaying god, this didn't go over so well with the many players who want those moments where your character feels considerably more powerful than their foes. While this still happens in the newer games, the gap between the strength of your character and the monsters is much smaller until you're decked out in high-level gear.

Level scaling seems to solve a lot of problems with maintaining a certain degree of challenge in the newer Diablo games, but it does diminish the spikes in power you can get from finding a particularly strong item or leveling up.

We already know Diablo 5 will return to procedurally-generating areas so that every dungeon, or open world zone, will look different every time you visit them—a crucial part of Diablo 2 that suggests Blizzard is interested in bringing back core elements from the series' history.

(Image credit: Future)Shely said level scaling in Diablo 5 isn't something the team has fully discussed yet, but acknowledged how important your character's power level is to the experience.

"Diablo is a game that, in many ways, is about your character getting stronger and when the monsters get stronger at the same time, especially outside of your control… You've filled the experience bar, you get stronger, you should feel awesome now, a wave of light pulses out from you, a bunch of monsters die," he explained. "That's wonderful, but then you're going to go hit some more monsters and you should feel powerful. And sometimes automatic scaling can get in the way of that feeling, which is so core to it, and that's why this is a really important question. And so, we're going to take a somewhat different approach to that in Diablo 5."

As someone who has never been a huge fan of level scaling in RPGs, it's nice to hear that Blizzard is willing to rethink a major component of the recent Diablo games. Newer action RPGs, like Path of Exile 2, are great examples of how friction, like running into monsters way too powerful for you, can make the grind for better and better loot more meaningful when there are actual risks.

Diablo 5 is set in a post-apocalyptic world where the demon lord has won. Finding a new sword that lets you crush the monsters who humiliated you a few levels earlier should emphasize the progress you've made on your journey to save Sanctuary from Hell's army. Blizzard says regular updates about the game's development will begin next year and that it will incorporate feedback along the way. I'll be curious to see exactly how level scaling—or the lack of it—will work and how far the dev team is willing to go to recreate the classic Diablo experience.

items.text:

Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson aren't enough to salvage Apple TV's new comedy series Brothers from being an uninspired and unfunny show. The main selling point of Brothers is, of course, the pairing of McConaughey and Harrelson. The two have had one of the longest and most visible bromances in Hollywood history. Between EDtv in 1999, Surfer, Dude in 2008, and True Detective season 1 in 2014, Harrelson and McConaughey have become a modern and more prolific version of Paul Newman and Robert Redford.

Brothers also has another real-world draw: Harrelson and McConaughey have teased that they may in fact be biological brothers. An old rumor asserts that McConaughey's mother knew Harrelson's father at the time the younger star was conceived, though McConaughey refuses to get a DNA test (via The Hollywood Reporter). While Brothers doesn't claim to offer any definitive answers about that rumor, its fictionalized story is based on the premise that they could be half-brothers with a shared father.

On top of that juicy family drama, Brothers puts a few new dramatic elements into play. McConaughey decides to run for governor of Texas, Harrelson and his family invade the former's ranch on their traveling tour bus, and many family sitcom shenanigans ensue. Unfortunately, Brothers forgot the comedy aspect of "situational comedy," and Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey won't be joining the halls of TV's best bromances any time soon.

Brothers Is A Pale Imitation Of Better Buddy Comedies & Family Sitcoms

​​​​​

The worst part about Brothers is that it’s simply not that funny. For a comedy show with such a powerhouse duo as Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey, I expected a lot. In the end, I was thoroughly disappointed. Brothers isn’t even as funny as True Detective, the pair’s most famous collaboration, and that show is primarily a gritty police procedural.

Brothers feels like an attempt at a classic sitcom in all the worst ways: tired tropes that have been done before and better, flat jokes that could have used a laugh track to clue the audience in on what’s supposed to be funny, and a very uncomfortable quasi-incestuous relationship. It seems like the writers of Brothers mashed Friends, Modern Family, and The White Lotus together into an unrecognizable gelatinous mass that’s less than the sum of its parts.

The weirdly incestuous relationship also deserves its own bit of criticism. In Brothers’ fictional versions of the families, McConaughey’s son, Wyatt (Nolan Almeida), and Harrelson’s daughter, Kai (Oona Yaffe), are essentially cousins. They grew up together as family friends, and there’s a chance, as the show’s premise advertises, that they’re actual cousins as well.

That doesn’t stop Brothers from giving them a young, budding romance or from very overtly declaring that Kai is adopted, so it’s okay for her to have a crush on the kid she’s treated as family her entire life. The whole subplot smacks of weirdness, and Brothers’ attempts to be meta about it and call the incest-coded relationship what it is do nothing to make it more palatable.

Even the connective tissue of Brothers, the “true rumor” of Harrelson investigating whether he’s related to McConaughey, can’t save it. That was a solid premise that had real-world intrigue, but I couldn’t help but feel Brothers would have been better executed as a reality show. At least then we could have gotten a definitive answer about their genealogy and a look at who these celebrities actually are. Instead, we’re left with what is essentially fan fiction about the two, and bad fan fiction at that.

Brothers also has very little original content to offer beyond its semi-true premise. So many of the show's episodes are built around mishaps and miscommunications that have defined sitcoms for decades. There's maybe a single episode in this season that didn't make me think I had seen another show, like Arrested Development or Malcolm in the Middle, do the same story better. Brothers is built on stale comedic situations, and it's not nearly inventive enough to make those situations entertaining.

One of the few redeeming qualities Brothers has at its disposal, the pairing of Harrelson and McConaughey, only works about half the time. At some points, that central duo is perfectly strange, lovable, and charismatic. Their real friendship drips through the fictional facade of their characters, and they have great chemistry. At other points, the pair are caricatures of themselves that are still, paradoxically, astroturfed to make the real men look good. The litany of plugs for McConaughey’s books and mentions of Harrelson’s anarchist politics got downright grating as Brothers went on.

Brothers is at its best when it leans into offbeat humor, but it never commits to the bit enough to cross the border from “occasionally amusing” to “genuinely funny.”

Unfortunately, the references to McConaughey and Harrelson’s respective filmographies may be the best part about Brothers. There are plenty of references to movies like Interstellar and Venom: Let There Be Carnage, and, of course, True Detective, that should delight their fans. It's also quite fun to see a reversal of their True Detective roles, with Harrelson taking the more zany oddball role while McConaughey plays the straight man. Those references are playful and fun, but they don’t lend much substance to Brothers beyond reminding the audience that the main characters are movie stars in the real world.

This should illustrate how much of a wasted opportunity pairing Harrelson with McConaughey was: my favorite character in Brothers was a surprise guest star. This mystery actor nails all of his scenes and stands head and shoulders above his castmates in comedic timing, delivery, and, most importantly, commitment to the bit. He wasn't even billed as one of Brothers' stars, yet he easily outshines Harrelson and McConaughey.

The most frustrating thing about Brothers is that there are inklings of a better show here. McConaughey and Harrelson are great when they’re allowed to be the butt of the joke and revel in the peculiarities of this Odd Couple pairing, like wearing matching blue cowboy tuxedos in the trailer for Brothers. Brothers is at its best when it leans into offbeat humor, but it never commits to the bit enough to cross the border from “occasionally amusing” to “genuinely funny.” That’s perhaps its greatest crime.

Brothers' Few Advantages Can't Make Up For Its Weaknesses

One of the only saving graces of Brothers is the many moments it takes to be more earnest than comedic. There are some great dramatic elements at play in Brothers. The fictionalized version of McConaughey has to grapple with his father's legacy. Harrelson's character has a checkered past as an absent father to his two daughters, and he makes great strides in making amends and reconnecting with his children.

Unfortunately, Brothers doesn't really dive into these character dynamics in earnest until it's nearly over. The first episodes are a slog of jokes that don't land and build up to the reveal of the truth behind the "true rumor." Once it gets there, Brothers handles its emotions and dramatic tension well, but it takes too long to get there.

Aside from Harrelson and McConaughey, Brothers also has some competent supporting actors. Holland Taylor is great as the zany, aging Ma Mac, and the members of the respective families are good. Ella Grace Helton, who plays McConaughey's daughter, also showed off some of the best comedic chops of the main cast. Lisa Gilroy was good, but like the rest of Brothers' humor, I wish she would have been let off the leash and allowed to showcase her usual weird comedic style.

Perhaps the highest praise I can give to Brothers is for its technical aspects. This show doesn't indulge in the overly gray and dark color grading and lighting so many shows in the streaming era fall victim to. Texas looks vibrant and beautiful, shots are well blocked and choreographed, and there's a very professional sheen to the entire series that never sacrifices warmth and familiarity. Brothers is one of the most visually pleasing sitcoms I've ever watched.

These few advantages aren't enough to salvage Brothers, however. At the end of the day, this was supposed to be a situational comedy, and it failed to be funny more times than I can forgive. There may have been a better version of this show before David West Read departed as Brothers' showrunner, but that's not the version we got. All in all, Brothers ended up closer to Surfer, Dude than True Detective in the ranking of Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson's collaborations.

Unfortunately, Brothers forgot the comedy aspect of "situational comedy," and Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey won't be joining the halls of TV's best bromances any time soon.
Brothers Is A Pale Imitation Of Better Buddy Comedies & Family Sitcoms

The worst part about Brothers is that it’s simply not that funny. For a comedy show with such a powerhouse duo as Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey, I expected a lot. In the end, I was thoroughly disappointed. Brothers isn’t even as funny as True Detective, the pair’s most famous collaboration, and that show is primarily a gritty police procedural.

Brothers feels like an attempt at a classic sitcom in all the worst ways: tired tropes that have been done before and better, flat jokes that could have used a laugh track to clue the audience in on what’s supposed to be funny, and a very uncomfortable quasi-incestuous relationship. It seems like the writers of Brothers mashed Friends, Modern Family, and The White Lotus together into an unrecognizable gelatinous mass that’s less than the sum of its parts.

The weirdly incestuous relationship also deserves its own bit of criticism. In Brothers’ fictional versions of the families, McConaughey’s son, Wyatt (Nolan Almeida), and Harrelson’s daughter, Kai (Oona Yaffe), are essentially cousins. They grew up together as family friends, and there’s a chance, as the show’s premise advertises, that they’re actual cousins as well.

That doesn’t stop Brothers from giving them a young, budding romance or from very overtly declaring that Kai is adopted, so it’s okay for her to have a crush on the kid she’s treated as family her entire life. The whole subplot smacks of weirdness, and Brothers’ attempts to be meta about it and call the incest-coded relationship what it is do nothing to make it more palatable.

Even the connective tissue of Brothers, the “true rumor” of Harrelson investigating whether he’s related to McConaughey, can’t save it. That was a solid premise that had real-world intrigue, but I couldn’t help but feel Brothers would have been better executed as a reality show. At least then we could have gotten a definitive answer about their genealogy and a look at who these celebrities actually are. Instead, we’re left with what is essentially fan fiction about the two, and bad fan fiction at that.

Brothers also has very little original content to offer beyond its semi-true premise. So many of the show's episodes are built around mishaps and miscommunications that have defined sitcoms for decades. There's maybe a single episode in this season that didn't make me think I had seen another show, like Arrested Development or Malcolm in the Middle, do the same story better. Brothers is built on stale comedic situations, and it's not nearly inventive enough to make those situations entertaining.

One of the few redeeming qualities Brothers has at its disposal, the pairing of Harrelson and McConaughey, only works about half the time. At some points, that central duo is perfectly strange, lovable, and charismatic. Their real friendship drips through the fictional facade of their characters, and they have great chemistry. At other points, the pair are caricatures of themselves that are still, paradoxically, astroturfed to make the real men look good. The litany of plugs for McConaughey’s books and mentions of Harrelson’s anarchist politics got downright grating as Brothers went on.
Brothers is at its best when it leans into offbeat humor, but it never commits to the bit enough to cross the border from “occasionally amusing” to “genuinely funny.”

Unfortunately, the references to McConaughey and Harrelson’s respective filmographies may be the best part about Brothers. There are plenty of references to movies like Interstellar and Venom: Let There Be Carnage, and, of course, True Detective, that should delight their fans. It's also quite fun to see a reversal of their True Detective roles, with Harrelson taking the more zany oddball role while McConaughey plays the straight man. Those references are playful and fun, but they don’t lend much substance to Brothers beyond reminding the audience that the main characters are movie stars in the real world.

This should illustrate how much of a wasted opportunity pairing Harrelson with McConaughey was: my favorite character in Brothers was a surprise guest star. This mystery actor nails all of his scenes and stands head and shoulders above his castmates in comedic timing, delivery, and, most importantly, commitment to the bit. He wasn't even billed as one of Brothers' stars, yet he easily outshines Harrelson and McConaughey.

The most frustrating thing about Brothers is that there are inklings of a better show here. McConaughey and Harrelson are great when they’re allowed to be the butt of the joke and revel in the peculiarities of this Odd Couple pairing, like wearing matching blue cowboy tuxedos in the trailer for Brothers. Brothers is at its best when it leans into offbeat humor, but it never commits to the bit enough to cross the border from “occasionally amusing” to “genuinely funny.” That’s perhaps its greatest crime.

Aside from Harrelson and McConaughey, Brothers also has some competent supporting actors. Holland Taylor is great as the zany, aging Ma Mac, and the members of the respective families are good. items.text:
Stargate SG-1 Switched Genres For Its Long-Awaited Return In Timekeepers, To Mixed Results

Published Sep 23, 2026, 3:00 AM EDT

Nicholas Becher is a gaming journalist with an MFA in Creative Writing from FAU. With extensive experience playing video games, he covers all forms of gaming content at Screen Rant, from breaking news to the latest fan theories. Most-played games range from Clair Obscur to Civ to Elden Ring to Halo 2 and beyond.

Stargate SG-1 remains one of science fiction television's defining cult classics, transforming the premise of 1994's Stargate movie into an expansive universe filled with alien civilizations and unforgettable characters. Running for 10 seasons across an entire decade from 1997 to 2007, the series helped turn Stargate into a full-on franchise, eventually spawning Stargate Atlantis, Stargate Universe, movies, games, and multiple other spin-offs.

Yet despite its devoted fanbase, the franchise has spent more than a decade struggling to find its way back to live-action television. Part of that comes down to changing ownership, with shifting studio priorities over the years and multiple revival attempts that never made it to the screen. Even a new Amazon MGM series announced in November 2025 was cancelled before production began in June 2026, although reports indicate the studio hasn't abandoned the IP altogether. Certainly, the existence of the video game Stargate: Timekeepers proves there's some life in the franchise yet.

For longtime fans, the wait to step through the Stargate and back into the SG-1 timeline finally came to an end, albeit in an unexpected new medium, and the long-awaited return also came with a surprising shift in genre. Unfortunately, fans have been a bit underwhelmed by Stargate SG-1's official return.

Stargate SG-1 Switches Genres Completely In Official Return

After years of waiting, Stargate SG-1 has technically made its official return with Stargate: Timekeepers, but in a genre completely unlike the television series fans remember. Released for PC on January 23, 2024, Timekeepers transforms SG-1 into a real-time tactics strategy game built around stealth and controlling a squad of specialists as opposed to the action-adventure format you'd expect from the show.

The return was a long time coming, as Stargate: Continuum, the final live-action adventure featuring the SG-1 team, released in 2008, meaning Timekeepers debuted more than 15 years after SG-1's last live-action story. Even in gaming, there had been an enormous gap, with Stargate SG-1: Unleashed releasing for mobile in 2013, making Timekeepers the first major new Stargate game in nearly 11 years.

Timekeepers also firmly connects itself to the original series, with a story that branches from the end of SG-1 Season 7. It begins during the Battle of Antarctica before following Commander Eva McCain and a new team through an original 14-mission campaign involving the Goa'uld, Jaffa Resistance, and Unas. It's an unusual continuation of SG-1, and one that has been met with very mixed reactions so far, with many fans not sold on the concept and others absolutely loving it.

Stargate: Timekeepers Reactions Have Been Mixed

Unfortunately, Stargate: Timekeepers hasn't proven to be the triumphant return to SG-1 that fans were hoping for. The game currently carries a "Mixed" rating on Steam, with only 60% of its low 198 counted user reviews being positive, highlighting just how divisive this new direction for the franchise has been.

Much of that division comes from the gameplay itself. Some negative Steam reviews criticize Timekeepers' heavy emphasis on stealth, with players taking issue with enemy AI, controls, limited customization, and the trial-and-error nature of missions. Some negative reviews argue that its stealth systems ultimately make encounters feel more like puzzles that need to be solved in a particular sequence than open-ended tactical scenarios.

There is plenty of praise as well, however, particularly from players who already enjoy games such as Commandos, Desperados 3, and Shadow Tactics. Positive reviewers have highlighted the level design, character abilities, nostalgic Stargate elements, and the simple pleasure of finally exploring the SG-1 universe again. Several also acknowledge its rough edges, including bugs and comparatively modest production values.

Timekeepers may be something of a niche return for Stargate, landing as a welcome revival for some longtime SG-1 fans, but hardly the universally embraced comeback many had spent years awaiting. That said, you can check it out on Steam now and see for yourself.

items.title: Unlike its stars, Brothers is only half-baked
items.author: Erik Adams
items.summary: If streaming-TV originals have a final form, it may be this: Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey playing fictionalized versions of themselves in what has
items.text:
If streaming-TV originals have a final form, it may be this: Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey playing fictionalized versions of themselves in what has to be the most expensive version of a 2010s ABC family sitcom ever made. An amusing-enough method of keeping Apple TV subscribers around between seasons of Ted Lasso and Stick, Brothers re-teams the-real life buds and True Detective stars in an alternately wholesome and profane Apple TV series that’s built around a tabloid anecdote and drafts off public personae the headlining talent previously plied in service of AI enterprise software.


Brothers’ laidback approach to telling the story of the Harrelson clan crashing at the McConaughey family ranch is held together by valiant efforts by some of the producers, writers, and directors behind the American Office, Modern Family, and New Girl. And yet when the sporadic laughter subsides, it’s hard not to see this celebrity-driven trifle as an indicator of the current state of TV that’s more accurate than any of the many awards Apple picked up during the night when the (possibly biological?) brothers of Brothers tried to get a rushed Emmys ceremony to the end of its timeslot through the sheer force of their combined charisma. And that’s all before self-anointed new king of Hollywood David Ellison’s name shows up in the credits.


Brothers is—per a title card that gets less cute and necessary (because who jumps into a streaming show midseason?) by the episode— “based on a true rumor” of a sexual encounter between Harrelson’s ne’er-do-well father and McConaughey’s mother (played here with plenty of southern-fried pluck by Holland Taylor). But the mystery of the Oscar winner’s paternity is mere logline window dressing for a show that’s more about the colliding worlds of two families and how those collisions prove that the bond of co-starring in Surfer, Dude is thicker than blood. It’s also, to varying degrees, a show about eldest Harrelson daughter Olive (Highdee Kuan) getting over a called-off engagement, her dad paying for the sins of his old man, and McConaughey making good on his idle thoughts of running for political office. The third of those plot lines is the most forced and farthest fetched, but it at least makes room for Lisa Gilroy to sprinkle a little Comedy Bang! Bang! weirdness into the proceedings as a high-strung campaign manager who upbraids Harrison and McConaughey in terms that, fortunately for Brothers, only kinda sorta encapsulate the show: “an endless barrage of egomaniacal and borderline sociopathic behavior from both of you.”


This is no vanity project. The leads allow themselves to look plenty foolish—particularly Harrelson, whose just slightly exaggerated personal beliefs and hippie-dippy flakiness make him a thorn in everyone on the ranch’s side. This also gives him a chance to tap into the comedic spirit of the last TV character he played who shared his first name; the golden retriever Woody Boyd energy that so frequently bolsters his performance here is a nice reminder that before Harrelson played hard-asses, deadbeats, and loose cannons on the big screen, he was one of the funniest supporting sitcom players of the ’80s. If nothing else Brothers is a fresh display of those particular talents.


Playing relatively straight man to the nomadic vegan bestie living out of the psychedelic bus in his driveway, McConaughey gets less color to play here. That’s in keeping with the poet-philosopher guise he’s donned since TV audiences first fell under the sway of Rust Cohle and his Big Hug Mug (a prop that’s too prominently displayed throughout Brothers to count as an Easter egg). But McConaughey’s corner of Brothers is more muted as a result, creating added strain for the campaign storyline, which, despite its Texas-size scale, lacks the more captivating personal stakes of what’s happening among the Harrelsons. McConaughey gets to cut loose in a few episodes with the Woodman, but of the two of them, he’s the one whose commitment to playing “himself” comes across as coasting.


Brothers lives in a hazy no-man’s land between “working vacation for movie stars” and “bingeable crowd-pleaser.” This is no slapdash production. The visuals capitalize on the natural splendor of the show’s Texas Hill Country setting; showrunner Lee Eisenberg hired plenty of names that will ring a bell for anyone who kept up with the vintage of network sitcom that Brothers most closely resembles. Between directors Trent O’Donnell, Erin O’Malley, and Jason Winer and writers Brett Baer, Dave Finkel, Alex Cuthbertson, and Matt Fusfeld, it feels like Eisenberg called his way down a New Girl alumni phone tree. (KPop Demon Hunters screenwriters Danya Jimenez and Hannah McMechan are aboard here too—for the most music-heavy episodes, naturally.) Every once in awhile, the experience in that writer’s room comes through loud and clear, as when Harrelson exchanges rat-a-tat with two old-timers trying to collect on a debt owed to them by his dad, or in a visual gag that reveals McConaughey’s incredibly involved grooming routines. Unfortunately, such material was placed in some run-of-the-mill scripts, with stock plots like Harrelson and McConaughey forgetting Valentine’s Day and paying a steep price for it.


Despite recalling comedies of days gone by, Brothers winds up feeling extremely contemporary—in mostly unflattering ways. It’s queue-filler of the highest order—TV-like product with megastar wattage. The half-hour episodes go down as easy as the craft brews McConaughey holds so conspicuously label-to-camera, but they lead to neither drunken comedic euphoria or regrettable “I can’t believe I watched the whole thing” hangover. There are some earnest attempts at fleshing out various family members and relationships—Harrelson and Kuan strike up a real tender dynamic while the scuttlebutt about Olive’s granddad and Ma Mac provides welcome distraction from her romantic woes. But there’s little sense of whether all that’s being developed there might continue to develop, or be worth developing, past this single season.


It’s not always funny, but Brothers is never not a curious artifact of an uneasy period in TV history, when one show can contain abundant f-bombs, some of the biggest bong rips ever put on television, and an adorable moppet putting her confidence to the test as she follows in her father’s footsteps and goes out for the school play. Yet as momentous as such events may be, there’s little sense of any of it impacting the characters in meaningful, long-lasting ways. To paraphrase the tagline for a movie whose iconography Brothers raids without shame or real thought (nobody raised an eyebrow at the sixth-episode school-dance invitation conducted in Wooderson cosplay?): We’re watching a time the fake Harrelsons and fake McConaugheys will never forget. If only we could remember anything about the show two or three months from now.


Erik Adams is The A.V. Club’s senior TV editor.

But McConaughey’s corner of Brothers is more muted as a result, creating added strain for the campaign storyline, which, despite its Texas-size scale, lacks the more captivating personal stakes of what’s happening among the Harrelsons. McConaughey gets to cut loose in a few episodes with the Woodman, but of the two of them, he’s the one whose commitment to playing “himself” comes across as coasting.

Brothers lives in a hazy no-man’s land between “working vacation for movie stars” and “bingeable crowd-pleaser.” This is no slapdash production. The visuals capitalize on the natural splendor of the show’s Texas Hill Country setting; showrunner Lee Eisenberg hired plenty of names that will ring a bell for anyone who kept up with the vintage of network sitcom that Brothers most closely resembles. Between directors Trent O’Donnell, Erin O’Malley, and Jason Winer and writers Brett Baer, Dave Finkel, Alex Cuthbertson, and Matt Fusfeld, it feels like Eisenberg called his way down a New Girl alumni phone tree. (KPop Demon Hunters screenwriters Danya Jimenez and Hannah McMechan are aboard here too—for the most music-heavy episodes, naturally.) Every once in awhile, the experience in that writer’s room comes through loud and clear, as when Harrelson exchanges rat-a-tat with two old-timers trying to collect on a debt owed to them by his dad, or in a visual gag that reveals McConaughey’s incredibly involved grooming routines. Unfortunately, such material was placed in some run-of-the-mill scripts, with stock plots like Harrelson and McConaughey forgetting Valentine’s Day and paying a steep price for it.

Despite recalling comedies of days gone by, Brothers winds up feeling extremely contemporary—in mostly unflattering ways. It’s queue-filler of the highest order—TV-like product with megastar wattage. The half-hour episodes go down as easy as the craft brews McConaughey holds so conspicuously label-to-camera, but they lead to neither drunken comedic euphoria or regrettable “I can’t believe I watched the whole thing” hangover. There are some earnest attempts at fleshing out various family members and relationships—Harrelson and Kuan strike up a real tender dynamic while the scuttlebutt about Olive’s granddad and Ma Mac provides welcome distraction from her romantic woes. But there’s little sense of whether all that’s being developed there might continue to develop, or be worth developing, past this single season.

It’s not always funny, but Brothers is never not a curious artifact of an uneasy period in TV history, when one show can contain abundant f-bombs, some of the biggest bong rips ever put on television, and an adorable moppet putting her confidence to the test as she follows in her father’s footsteps and goes out for the school play. Yet as momentous as such events may be, there’s little sense of any of it impacting the characters in meaningful, long-lasting ways. To paraphrase the tagline for a movie whose iconography Brothers raids without shame or real thought (nobody raised an eyebrow at the sixth-episode school-dance invitation conducted in Wooderson cosplay?): We’re watching a time the fake Harrelsons and fake McConaugheys will never forget. If only we could remember anything about the show two or three months from now.
Erik Adams is The A.V. Club’s senior TV editor.

items.title: Where can Australians buy R18+ PC games without a credit card? Pretty much everywhere but Steam
items.author: shaun.prescott@futurenet.com (Shaun Prescott)

items.text:
Valve implemented age verification for Australian Steam users earlier this month, which was inevitable: Australian law demands it. Unfortunately, Valve has opted for the most brute force, user-negligent approach possible. To buy R18+ games on Steam in Australia—to even access their store pages—you need to provide a credit card.

The problem being that most Australians don't use credit cards. This study of consumer payment behaviour by the Reserve Bank of Australia bears this out: the share of payments made in Australia with credit or card charges in 2025 was 23% (versus debit cards at 49%).

This is in stark contrast with the US where, according to Bankrate, 74% of adults own a credit card (and nearly half of those are in debt!).

I'm not sure if Valve did its research: perhaps it did and it doesn't care. Rather than create the infrastructure to cope with age verification on Steam, or pay a contractor to do it, it's probably easier for Valve to let Australian customers be angry about it. I've received emails from Australian banks flummoxed by the sudden rush of inbound customer calls about this policy. One asked me, rather desperately: has Valve hinted at the possibility of other verification methods? (Do marmots eat Coco Pops for breakfast? Valve won't hint: one day it'll just suddenly happen.)

I've reached out to Valve on this matter but not heard back. So what to do in the meantime? The only option you really have at the moment is to take your business elsewhere, or buy Steam codes from legitimate third-party sellers.

But how do other shopfronts handle age verification? I offer the below advice not to aide young'uns in their desire to play Doom Eternal, but to help actual adults who don't have a credit card. And, of course, the alternatives below are not guaranteed to stock all R18+ games, with GTA 5 being an especially notable example.

Let's have a look:

No credit card required PC gaming shopfronts

Epic Games Store
Do you need a credit card to buy R18+ games? ❌

Epic Games Store uses KWS (Kids Web Services) for age verification. There are three available options: a Face scan (via Yoti), using a Credit Card (via Stripe), or ID Scan, which can include a driver's license, passport or government-issued ID.

GOG
Do you need a credit card to buy R18+ games? ❌

GOG doesn't have an age verification system for Australian users at the moment, though that will likely change at the drop of a hat.

Xbox | Microsoft Store
Do you need a credit card to buy R18+ games? ❌

Microsoft uses the usual array of age verification options: face scan (via Yoti), email (VerifyMy) or official document such as licence, passport, or government ID.

No credit card required PC gaming key sellers

At time of writing, third-party key sellers Fanatical and Green Man Gaming don't prompt Australians to prove their age when purchasing R18+ games. That's nice, but whether Fanatical or Green Man Gaming are actually selling the R18+ games you want is another matter: both are selling, for example, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, but neither sell Grand Theft Auto 5.

Fanatical
Do you need a credit card to buy R18+ games? ❌
Is age verification required? ❌

Fanatical has R18+ games like Rimworld and the most recent Metal Gear Solid Volume 2 collection. Buying through Fanatical grants a Steam key which can be redeemed on Steam.

Green Man Gaming
Do you need a credit card to buy R18+ games? ❌
Is age verification required? ❌

GMG has heaps of R18+ games but, crucially, not Grand Theft Auto 5 (though don't you own that already anyway?). Buying through GMG grants a Steam key which can be redeemed on Steam.

Can I use a VPN to buy R18+ games on Steam?

Valve's subscriber agreement is very clear about this: using a VPN to buy R18+ games in Australia without verifying your age can result in account termination.

"You agree that you will not use IP proxying or other methods to disguise the place of your residence, whether to circumvent geographical restrictions on game content, to order or purchase at pricing not applicable to your geography, or for any other purpose," the agreement reads.

"If you do this, Valve may terminate your access to your Account."

items.title: Prebuilt Steam Machine faceplate screens are here, delivering decent, surprisingly cheaper alternatives to Valve-approved DIY builds
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: If you own a Steam Machine, and still cling to the misconception that my budget faceplate ideas aren’t good enough for you, you basically have three options
items.text:
If you own a Steam Machine, and still cling to the misconception that my budget faceplate ideas aren’t good enough for you, you basically have three options for front panel customisation. The first is to grab something off Etsy or suchlike. The second is take advantage of Valve’s open-source Inkterface project to build yourself an E-Ink display, onto which you can electronically daub performance monitoring info. The third is to end up with more or less the same panel as option two, but have someone else make it for you. That’s what arch accessory makers JSAUX are proposing with their Steam Machine E-Ink and Pixel Matrix faceplates, which go on sale today after a few weeks of preening around the case mod scene.

I’ve been using both on my Machine at home, and they’re quite good fun. The E-Ink faceplate, for which I sense the greater internet buzz, is a crisp, tidy little black-and-white panel, while the PixelMatrix trades detail density for colour and retro charm. Both have a few different display modes, switchable in SteamOS’s quick settings menu (via some clever integration with the Decky Loader plugin tool), and while I had to set this up manually, JSAUX say the requisite software will be downloadable via Steam itself from early October. Truly, it’s all the results of a DIY mod and more, conveniently pre-prepared for people who don’t own soldering irons.

Of the two, I narrowly prefer the PixelMatrix, that favouritism expanding significantly when using a faceplate for performance monitoring. The E-Ink model is pretty knackered in this respect, as its fastest refresh speed option is a hardly widowmaking once per minute, and I’m rarely interested in what my Steam Machine’s GPU was doing sixty seconds ago. I also, uh, like how the sun is actually yellow on the PixelMatrix’s weather view. This is apparently what RPS hardware coverage has come to.

Tell you what, here’s a cat picture. One advantage the E-Ink screen has over the dot matrix is that it makes much, much more sense for turning the Steam Machine into a digital photo frame; this holiday snap of a stray Baku resident was just too detailed for the PixelMatrix’s chunky LEDs to recognisably reproduce. The latter might work for pics of your favourite Jenga block, or perhaps an ironic, front-on photo of the Steam Machine itself, but for anything with eyes or hair you’re better off with the E-Ink.

Granted, this isn’t the only shortcoming. I find it disproportionately annoying that the outer edges – on both faceplates – don’t quite line up perfectly with the USB/power button/ light strip section on the Machine’s bottom lip, and the right-sided USB-C port on the E-Ink panel forces the connecting cable to stretch unattractively across the same section. The FPS 'counter' on each screen’s performance monitors also downright misleads: it displays your TV/monitor’s refresh rate, in frames-per-second instead of Hz, and not actual in-game performance. It wouldn’t be very useful to get a once-per-minute framerate update on the E-Ink model anyway, but still.

At least when the E-Ink screen does refresh, though, it does so faster and less distractingly than Valve’s Inkterface design. A design which, if you follow the instructions by the book, will also give you a single performance monitoring screen, not the choice of performance, play time tracking, clock, weather, calendar, or photo frame modes that JSAUX’s ready-made screens have out of the box. And, in a major break from PC hardware convention, they both work out cheaper than taking the DIY option.

Now, "cheaper" doesn’t necessarily mean "cheap" - the E-Ink is $100 and the PixelMatrix is $90, or roughly a tenth of the infamously ‘spenny Machine it latches onto. These are undoubtedly luxuries, for those who didn’t already blow their entire luxury budget on miniature PCs. Yet totting up the combined component prices of what you’d need for an Inkerface panel reveals it to cost $104.50, not including the expense of either 3D-printing the external housing or buying something pre-printed for an additional 15 dollaridoos.

In a sense, then, the $100, sub-6in greyscale screen that only refreshes once a minute is... good value. Weird! But probably fine. Now I cross my fingers and hope Valve don’t kill it off in a few days’ time, like the last Steam Machine accessory I tried.

items.title: What's on PC Gamer's desk?
items.author: James Bentley
items.summary: I'm of the opinion that your desk space says a lot about you. Be it that you care more about function than style, or you like Hatsune Miku just a tad too
items.text:
I'm of the opinion that your desk space says a lot about you. Be it that you care more about function than style, or you like Hatsune Miku just a tad too much.

I'm also of the opinion that someone's desk space speaks volumes about their real life, like one person may be efficient in other areas, or another must just really, really like Hatsune Miku.

As such, I tasked the bravest of my coworkers with sharing photos of their desk spaces, alongside some fun facts, because I'm nosy like that.

If you are as nosy as I am, here's what some of the PC Gamer team have on their desks. And you can even vote on your favourite desk below.

Evan Lahti, Strategic Director

FutureRig details: RTX 3080, 32 GB DDR4 RAM, curved ultrawide 3440x1440p monitor, an Uplift standing desk, use two mice, split gaming keyboard, Bose SoundLink Mini speaker, have had the same Corsair cube case for 11 years

I need to replace my 650W power supply with a 750W+, which has been causing some first-person games to hard crash when there are power spikes

I sometimes use a balance board at my standing desk to recreate my San Francisco skateboarding days

I am a big fan of Speks' line of fidget equipment

Mollie Taylor, Features Producer

FutureFutureRig details: Nvidia GeForce RTX3070, AMD Ryzen 9 3900XT, 32 GB RAM.

Fun facts: Vertical monitor is exclusively to service my crippling rhythm game addiction (Sound Voltex)

I'm a two-mouse gal (one for MMOs, one for FPS of course)

This is probably the least tchotchke'd out the wazoo my desk has been in months

Jacob Ridley, Managing Editor, Hardware

FutureFutureFutureFutureFutureRig details: RTX 5080, Ryzen 7 7900X, Wooting 80HE, Noctua desk fan, Schiit DAC/amp w/ Audeze LCD-S20, an incredibly fashionable light-up mouse pad, Razer Ergo mouse/Viper V4 Pro.

No amount of regular cleaning can contain the quantity of cat hair on my desk

I once used a sensor that told me how many times I used my standing desk to actually stand during the day but I unplugged it because I didn't like the results

I have a timer on my desk to try and maintain my focus for longer but my internet-addled brain might be too gone to save at this point

I also have two mice, which from the looks of this list, is not a fun fact at all. It's 100% expected behaviour

Issy van der Velde, PC Gaming Show deputy editor

(Image credit: Future)Rig details: Work-provided ThinkPad, a mouse I "borrowed" from a friend many years ago, mouse pad my girlfriend had spare.

I like to keep things minimal

Joshua Wolens, News Writer

FutureFutureRig details: RTX 4080, 5800X3D, 32 GB DDR4 RAM, mechanical keyboard I got from eBay sometime around the Teapot Dome scandal, one (1) mouse.

I only have one mouse, which did not heretofore feel like a thing worth pointing out but apparently marks me as a freak

I actually much prefer to do work on my Mac (pictured) while sprawled on the settee—and I prefer to play games that way too; my PC is hooked up to my TV—so I don't actually spend all that much time here outside of meetings

Important: I have a bronze Soviet bust of Marx and Lenin that I got at Izmailovsky Market that would be here if my desk weren't colonised by stupid devices that require charging. Imagine they're there for me. Thank you

Speaking of which, moving my charging gear out of my bedroom and onto my desk was the best choice I ever made, as it meant I stopped taking my phone to bed and now actually get to sleep on time. Recommended!

Dave James, EIC hardware

FutureRig details: Hyte Y70 Touch, RTX 5090, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, 64 GB RAM, Gigabyte Aorus 32-inch OLED, Dough Spectrum 27-inch IPS (portrait, important), Mountain Everest 60 keyboard, Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro, Steam Controller (the good one), Kanto Ora speakers, Dezctop standing desk.

My fishtank PC is filled with the D&D Lego minifigs collection

I recently replaced my motherboard because the ASRock board was doing weird things. And it booted first time afterwards. Weird

I'm really bad at cooling my PC, and my CPU has to be actively screaming for me to up the fan speed from 'Quiet'. I think some of the Lego minifigs have started to melt

Midas, Video Producer

FutureFutureRig details: RTX 5070ti, 32 GB RAM, AMD AM5 Ryzen 7 9800X3D - Tryx Panorama SE 360MM ARGB AIO Liquid Cooler.

I have the coolest RGB set-up, but my wire management is beyond trash—no peeking behind the desk

I’m a PC Gamer, but I don’t W,A,S,D—I have a drawer full of controllers. My keyboard and mouse are just for editing

Widescreen monitor only! Sorry, not sorry

Fraser Brown, Online Editor

FutureFutureRig details: RTX 4090, Intel i9-13900k, 32 GB RAM.

Also on my desk:

A bust of a cockapoo, which I use to hold my sunglasses

A medieval helmet, which I put my hats on

Assorted Lego

Pins

Junk

Jake Tucker, Editorial Director, PC Gaming Show

(Image credit: Future)Rig details: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, RXT 4080, 32 GB memory.

Half of my desk is taken up by my FLX4 DJ controller, because apparently I'm having a midlife crisis after I picked one up as a hobby a year ago. I'm about to upgrade to an all-in-one unit, and I'm scared of how much of my desk that will colonise

I was given the mousemat as a gift and after declaring a glass mousemat too fancy to use, I now can't use anything else

I've spent the last five years trying to find a sound setup I like, even moving to in-ear monitors for a bit. The SteelSeries Nova Pro headset has finally won out because charging batteries is easy to do with the on-desk control station. I need a wireless headset too because my ADHD brain makes me get up and walk off from my desk when I'm loading into games or matching and I keep garroting myself with the headphone wires

I, too, am just now learning that everyone I work with uses a collection of mice for different tasks and I do not like it

Andy Edser, Hardware Writer

FutureFutureFutureFutureRig details: RTX 5070 Ti, AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, 32 GB DDR5, custom Glorious GMMK 3 keyboard, Logitech MX Master 4, Fractal Design Scape, Audeze Maxwell 2, Razer Wolverine V3 controller, Razer Cobra HyperSpeed, 32-inch 4K BenQ Mini-LED monitor.

See that little doohickey behind my mouse? It's a cooling gel wrist rest I've cut out of a lesser mouse pad so I can move it around my desk

I use a single 32-inch 4K monitor, as the good lord intended

I have two gaming headsets, and two mice. The Logitech MX Master 4 and Fractal Design Scape are my daily drivers, while the Razer squeaker and the Audeze Maxwell 2 are for serious business gaming

The most useful things on my desk are the little block of neon green post-it notes and the Sharpie pen. I write things down because I'm getting old now and my brain looks like a block of Swiss cheese

Oh yeah, that speaker placement—I use headphones when I'm in front of the PC, while the speakers are for playing loud music across the rest of the room. I am wonderful to live with, and my neighbours are big fans

Tim Clark, Group Editorial Director, Games

FutureFutureRig details: iBUYPOWER HYTE Y70 RGB, Intel Core i9-14900KF, 32.0 GB memory, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, 2 TB storage. Alienware 34 240Hz QD-OLED, NuPhy Air96 Wireless Mechanical Keyboard, G903 Lightspeed wireless mouse, Xbox Elite Series 2 Controller, Ora by Kanto, Razer Seiren mini.

The two rectangular lights on my desk use dimmable Hue bulbs, which are great for making you look less dug up on calls

Though I don't stand that much these days, the Uplift Standing desk was a huge upgrade to the office

I have an enormous digital clock right in my eyeline because I am a fiend for losing track of time

I also have a couple of scented candles because I am bougie and confident in my masculinity

Jess Kinghorn, Hardware Writer

(Image credit: Future)Rig details: iBuyPower RDY Y40 Valorant VCTA R003, AMD Ryzen 7 7700X 8-Core Processor, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 SUPER, 32.0 GB memory, 1 TB storage.

I really wasn't joking about my army of Miku Hatsune figurines

Believe it or not, I actually tidied up for this photo. This is what I mean when I describe my desk as 'cluttered'

I did have the Creative Stage Pro for sound, but that's been commandeered for the living room. That leaves me with only headphones, jumping out of my skin every time someone tries to get my attention

I also bought one of the Govee x Evangelion gaming light kits based on our review, but I've not set it up yet. I think the best gaming set ups ought to feel a bit like you're piloting a giant robot

You can't see it on account of the Be Quiet! Light Mount TKL, but my mouse pad features cool art from 2019's Control—specifically this image

James Bentley, Hardware Writer (that's me!)

(Image credit: Future)Rig details: Ryzen 7 7800X3D, RTX 4070 Super, 32 GB memory, Turtle Beach Stealth Pro II, Audeze LCD-S20, 8BitDo Retro R8, GameSir G7 Pro 8K, one 1440p OLED monitor and one 1080p IPS monitor. Creative XF1. Epomaker HE75 V2 TMR.

Yes, I am hoisting one monitor on the Creative speakers, and I only feel a little bad

That red block is from Naraka: Bladepoint, a game I quite enjoyed for about two weeks, and then decided never to go back to

Though I no longer use the NZXT speakers, I do still use the NZXT Switch Mix, hence the two pairs of headphones.

I love charging docks

items.title: I taught an old man new tunes in rhythm-action shopkeeper sim Mr. Records, and now you can try the demo yourself
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: One of the bright spots of a miserably grey Summer Game Fest 2026 was Mr. Records, a mashup of rhythm-action autorunner and casual vinyl shop management by
items.text:
One of the bright spots of a miserably grey Summer Game Fest 2026 was Mr. Records, a mashup of rhythm-action autorunner and casual vinyl shop management by music game specialists Glee-Cheese Studio. I’ve since played a demo – which you can now try yourself on Steam – and was pleased by the apparent confirmation that it can induce that head-nodding, foot-tapping thing that rhythm games should. Big fan, usually, of games that force me into involuntary body movements.

Watch on YouTube

Mr. Records follows George, a crusty but friendly old music aficionado in the process of establishing his own records boutique. Before putting a new song on the shelves, George insists on giving it a private listen, which sinks him into fantasy platforming sequences where successful jumps, slides, and throws are exclusively made on the beat. The next morning, punters show up asking for help finding a specific record, a task to which George – head still swollen with last night’s melodic discoveries – can apply his newfound knowledge.

Of this double A-side approach, I found the rhythm component the better bop. Its 2D button-tapping keeps it simpler than a Hi-Fi Rush or Metal: Hellsinger, but the mixing-up of jumps and slides and kicks quickly establishes the action as the kind where a momentary lapse in concentration can irreparably muck up your timing. Hence, head-nodding and foot-tapping.

George’s daydreams also have their own, colourful charm, scrolling along like the Yellow Submarine video by way of Thank Goodness You’re Here. Environments take inspiration from the song they accompany, so a breezy pop number might lead you through fields of dancing pastel flowers, while a fuzzy electronic track is all purple and pulsing. Well, maybe not all, as transitions between sections of a song may have a corresponding visual or mechanical shift that lasts only for that section – potentially including George's movement orientation being flipped sideways or upside down. Which is as disorienting as trying to play a guitar back to front, but also a good sign that Glee-Cheese have engineered every step of George’s wanderings to lock in with the flow of the music.

The songs in question are also entirely original, composed and recorded in-house. They’re a diverse bunch, the tracks I played through spanning psychedelic pop, classic rock and R&B-inspired rap (among others), and most have a lyrical whimsy to them that pairs well with the cartoon visuals. There’s some decently catchy earworms in there too, though the one song that lodged itself deepest within my head was also the one I most wanted rid of: a sausage-themed comedy tune whose chestless, too-close-to-the-mic crooning was and remains the stuff of nightmares. Thankfully, the rest of the soundtrack seems to be inoffensive at worst and jolly good fun at best, and the breadth of genres bodes well for George's dreamscape variety.

The shop management/social puzzling side, I imagine, needs more time to show its stuff. It’s based around recommending the right record based on customers’ vague, partial descriptions, but in the early stages I played, the challenge of digging up the correct vinyl was undermined by a lack of stock. George’s grand opening makes all of two records available, a business plan that would probably kill Claude from The Apprentice on the spot, and it looks like you’ll only be adding one or two records per night.

Also, and this is for sure a limitation of the demo/preview format, I could only see the shoots of the shopkeeping’s relationship-building aspect. Despite the lack of choice, it seems George does pick up some repeat customers, and it sounds like cultivating friendships with the regulars may prove more important than the shop’s balance sheet.

I’m interested to see where that goes, mind, as I am for George’s own story. A greyed puffin whose primary companion is a nap-happy dog, he has the air of someone to whom life hasn’t always been kind, even as he continues to appreciate and find solace in its artistic pleasures. Fortunately, this love of music is clearly shared by the game as a whole, which is exactly what you want when half of it is spent hitting buttons to an imaginary metronome.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.
